column2: A sedimentary rock made of calcium carbonate — the raw material nature uses for cliffs, and humans use for monuments.
An ornamental ruffled frill on the front of a shirt or dress — a wardrobe detail capable of upstaging its wearer.
The positively charged antiparticle of the electron — its scientific twin that took a rather different view on electricity.
The physicist famed for a feline thought experiment — the reason people endlessly debate the fate of a cat that isn't even there.
The pioneering Russian botanist and geneticist who travelled the globe collecting crop seeds to safeguard the future of farming.
America's first president and the name of its capital — a single word serving as both a historical figure and a political address.
An uncharged subatomic particle residing in the atomic nucleus — the proton's strictly neutral next-door neighbour.
A positively charged particle inside the atomic nucleus — a tiny carrier of a plus sign with huge sway over an element's chemistry.
A ghostly subatomic particle that barely interacts with matter, zipping straight through entire planets without stopping.
The largest planet in our solar system — a gas giant boasting a Great Red Spot and a gravitational ego to match.
The ancient Greek goddess of wisdom and warfare — patroness of those who prefer to think before charging into battle.
The capacity to reason, understand and solve problems — handy when brute force and luck have both shrugged their shoulders.
The body's largest internal organ, filtering toxins and working silent overtime after every festive banquet.
A masked ball or costume party where recognising an old friend is harder than finding an excuse to wear sequins.
The steady directional flow of water — the river's quiet reminder that it doesn't particularly care where you planned to swim.
A tradesperson who grinds grain into flour, turning golden ears of wheat into the raw promise of bread.
A building or machine equipped to grind grain — where harvested wheat completes its journey from field to flour.
Moving to a new home — a life event after which cardboard boxes are treated as permanent family members for months.
A large container for storing liquid or fuel — a vessel most deeply appreciated when it isn't running on empty.
Fine sediment settled on the bed of a river or lake — humble mud hiding remarkable fertility.
A valveless brass wind instrument whose crisp call rouses a camp faster than any megaphone.
Pierce, the Irish actor who played James Bond with an immaculate dinner jacket and a wry smile.
Sean, the Scottish screen legend who defined 007 with a tuxedo, a raised eyebrow and a signature brogue.
The indecisive Prince of Denmark who staged the world's most famous monologue opposite poor Yorick's skull.
Shakespeare's tragic Moorish general whose fatal jealousy could have been prevented by one calm conversation.
Othello's faithful, innocent wife in Shakespeare's tragedy — handed the saddest role in Venetian drama.
The romantic heroine of Alexander Grin's novella who waited faithfully for a ship with scarlet sails despite the neighbours' mockery.
Shakespeare's lovestruck young Montague of Verona, who turned evening balcony visits into an extreme sport.
A steam-powered railway veteran that hauled carriages across continents long before diesel or overhead wires arrived.
An underground or underwater passage bored through rock — a shortcut that begins with a stretch of total darkness.
A structure spanning a river, gorge or road — allowing you to reach the other side without growing wings.
A mechanical railway signal with movable arms that directs trains without ever blowing a whistle.
The inventor of the dot-and-dash telegraph code who taught messages to tap their way across oceans.
The founder of psychoanalysis, thanks to whom every innocent slip of the tongue suddenly looks deeply suspicious.
The title character of Vladimir Nabokov's controversial novel, whose name entered everyday vocabulary amid endless debate.
The Russian-American novelist behind 'Lolita' and 'Pale Fire' — a master prose stylist equally lethal at chess.
An imperial unit of distance equal to 1,609 metres — the reason your speedometer occasionally speaks a foreign language.
The SI unit of electrical resistance — a short name for the stubborn force stopping electric current from rushing straight through.
A poetic or archaic word for the eye, lending a touch of old-fashioned grandeur to anatomy.
The contemporary Russian postmodern satirist whose novels leave readers wondering if reality itself is a clever simulation.
The celebrated Russian realist painter who immortalised the gruelling toil of the Volga barge haulers.
The Renaissance painter, inventor and polymath who seemed to lack nothing except a quiet evening off.
The German Baroque master of fugues and chorales, whose music makes even strict mathematical counterpoint sound majestic.
The Polish Romantic composer and pianist famous for nocturnes and mazurkas that know how to sigh with elegance.
The German musical titan who composed his monumental Ninth Symphony even after losing his hearing.
The German Romantic composer of symphonies and Hungarian Dances, blending fiery passion with classical discipline.
The Austrian composer who wrote over six hundred lieder, turning brief vocal miniatures into towering art.
The Italian Baroque violinist and composer of 'The Four Seasons', who taught an orchestra how to perform the weather.
The anthropologist and author of the Don Juan books, after which readers never looked at desert cacti quite the same way.
A pair of concave wooden shells clicked together in the palm — the percussive heartbeat of Spanish flamenco.
The smallest unit of digital data, holding either a 0 or a 1 — the microscopic brick of the entire digital world.
A standard unit of digital storage made of eight bits — a tiny mouthful of data on the way to gigabytes.
A unit of text processed by a language model — the digital morsel of meaning AI counts on every prompt.
A colossal, tentacled sea monster of Nordic legend — basically an octopus that finds the ocean slightly cramped.
The loud, rumbling soundtrack of deep sleep — a midnight concert for which your bedfellow never bought a ticket.
A soft, fluffy plant fibre spun into breathable fabric — the humble hero behind your favourite T-shirt.
A flower-child of the 1960s counterculture who firmly believed peace signs beat marching boots every time.
Outer shine, refinement and immaculate grooming — the finishing touch turning an ordinary outfit into a red-carpet entrance.
A heavy iron lever with a curved tip that doesn't ask a jammed door to open — it invites it to reconsider.
The 19th-century Russian Romantic poet and author of 'A Hero of Our Time', where even mountain landscapes drip with drama.
A spiral-bladed drilling tool for boring holes into earth, wood or ice — a persistent helper that prefers working under pressure.
The Polish sci-fi philosopher who wrote 'Solaris', sending astronauts to worlds where alien intelligence refuses to make sense.
The English philologist and author of 'The Lord of the Rings', who invented entire Elvish languages just so hobbits had somewhere to live.
The American sci-fi visionary behind 'Fahrenheit 451', whose warnings about the future always felt uncomfortably human.
The American sci-fi master of cosmic irony, famous for dropping ordinary heroes into absurd universes and billing them for the trip.
The Russian historical painter behind 'Boyarynya Morozova', turning dramatic chapters of old Russia into monumental canvases.
The Russian painter, explorer and mystic whose luminous Himalayan landscapes look like portals to another realm.
Stephen, the American master of horror behind 'It' and 'The Shining', who ruined birthday clowns for an entire generation.
A specialist mariner who guides ships safely through tricky harbours and channels, knowing the riverbed better than the captain knows the bridge.
